en: The pointed beak of a Philippine hornbill acts as a wedge to crack open hard nuts.
The rough bark of a Narra tree increases friction, helping small insects climb its trunk.
Gravity pulls the water of Maria Cristina Falls downward to spin turbines and generate electricity.
Some dark sand grains on Philippine beaches contain magnetite, a naturally magnetic iron mineral.
Lightning is a massive spark of static electricity jumping between clouds during a tropical thunderstorm.
Rainbows form when sunlight refracts and reflects inside spherical raindrops after a heavy rain shower.
Fruit bats in Philippine caves use sound echoes to locate flying insects in complete darkness.
Dark volcanic sand on the slopes of Mayon volcano absorbs more radiant heat from the sun than light sand.
The sloping trail up Mount Pulag acts as an inclined plane, reducing the force needed to climb.
Tall turbines at the Bangui Wind Farm convert the kinetic energy of sea breezes into electricity.
Solar panels in sunny Batanes convert radiant energy from the sun directly into electrical energy.
The gravitational pull of the Moon on Earth's oceans creates the daily tides in Manila Bay.
